firebase-genkit:
Genkit is Google's open-source framework for adding generative AI features to apps: prompt management, flows, tool calling, retrieval (RAG) and evaluation, with plugins for Gemini, Vertex AI, OpenAI-compatible models and vector stores. It runs on Node.js, Go and Python and deploys easily to Firebase or Cloud Run.

Use this list when you move from a first prototype to a real feature. Start with **Plugins** to see which models and databases are supported, then go to **Tutorials** and **Talks** for end-to-end examples you can adapt.
billing:
Billing looks simple until you have to handle taxes, proration, refunds, multiple currencies and usage-based plans. This list collects material on pricing strategy, product catalogs, invoicing, accounting, marketplaces and fraud prevention for anyone building or running a paid product.

It is useful for founders deciding how to charge, developers integrating a payment provider, and finance teams reviewing their stack. Read **Basics** and **Pricing** first; the later sections go deeper into accounting, forecasting and compliance.
uno-platform:
Uno Platform lets .NET developers write a single C# and XAML codebase that runs on Windows, iOS, Android, macOS, Linux and the browser through WebAssembly. It is an alternative to .NET MAUI and Avalonia that reuses the WinUI API surface.

This list gathers samples, libraries, tools and live apps built with Uno. If you are evaluating it, check **Live apps** and **Open-source apps** to see real production results, then use **Samples** and **Libraries** to start your own project.
neuroscience:
This collection connects programming with the study of the brain and nervous system: software for analysing neural recordings and imaging, simulation tools, open datasets, courses and reading material.

It is aimed at researchers and students who code, and at developers curious about computational neuroscience. The **Programming** section lists the main Python and MATLAB toolkits; **Resources** points to courses, books and communities to learn the theory behind them.
raspberry-pi:
The Raspberry Pi is a low-cost single-board computer used for learning to code, home automation, media centres, robotics, retro gaming and small servers. This list covers the different models, operating system images, tools, project ideas and communities around it.

If you are buying your first board, compare the **Models** section before choosing. Then pick an image from **OS Images** and browse **Projects** for step-by-step builds you can finish in a weekend.
boilerplate-projects:
A good boilerplate saves days of setup: folder structure, build tools, linting, testing and deployment already wired together. This list groups starter projects by technology, from Android and iOS to JavaScript, Python, PHP, Ruby and microservices.

Before adopting one, check that it is still maintained and matches the versions you plan to use. A boilerplate is a starting point; remove what you don't need instead of carrying unused dependencies into production.
apache-wicket:
Apache Wicket is a component-based Java web framework where pages are built from plain HTML templates and reusable Java components, with state handled on the server. It is popular in enterprise and government applications that value type safety and long-term stability.

This list collects documentation, component libraries, integrations and IDE tools. Start with **Generic Info** for guides and books, then look at **Libraries** for ready-made components such as tables, charts and Bootstrap themes.
vagrant:
Vagrant, by HashiCorp, creates reproducible development environments: one configuration file describes a virtual machine, and every developer on the team gets the same setup with a single `vagrant up`. It works with VirtualBox, VMware, Hyper-V, Docker and cloud providers.

Here you will find base boxes, provisioning options, popular plugins and helper tools. Today many teams use containers or Dev Containers for the same job; Vagrant is still a solid choice when you need a full virtual machine with its own kernel.
functional-programming:
Functional programming builds software from pure functions, immutable data and composition. The ideas come from languages like Haskell, Lisp and ML, but they are now everyday tools in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Kotlin and Scala.

This list focuses on functional programming for JavaScript developers: utility libraries, languages that compile to JavaScript (Elm, PureScript, ReasonML and others), tools and learning resources. If you are new to the topic, begin with **Resources** before picking a library.
creative-tech-events:
Creative technology sits between code, art, design and music: generative visuals, installations, live coding, interactive media and new tools for creators. This list collects festivals, conferences and meetups around the world where that community meets.

Events are grouped by region, including Central and South America. Dates and formats change every year, so confirm on each official site before planning a trip or submitting a talk.
bluetooth-beacons:
Bluetooth Low Energy beacons are small transmitters that let phones detect proximity, used for indoor navigation, retail promotions, asset tracking and attendance. The two main formats are Apple's iBeacon and Google's Eddystone.

This list covers both standards, the Physical Web, installation and radio planning, configuration tools and scanner apps. If you are planning a deployment, read **Installation & Radio Planning** first: placement and interference matter more than the hardware brand.
steam-deck:
Valve's Steam Deck is a handheld PC running SteamOS, a Linux-based system with desktop mode, Proton compatibility for Windows games and support for emulators and third-party launchers.

The list covers guides, accessories, software, performance tuning, customization, battery management and emulation. New owners should start with **Guide** and **Performance**; the **Customization** and **Emulation** sections are where the Deck becomes a much more flexible device.
substrate:
Substrate is the Rust framework from Parity used to build custom blockchains, including Polkadot and its parachains. It provides modular building blocks called FRAME pallets for accounts, governance, staking and smart contracts, so teams can focus on their own logic.

This list gathers documentation, templates, pallets, framework extensions, talks and community channels. Rust experience is assumed; if you are new to blockchain development, read the **Resources** section and start from a template rather than from scratch.
coderabbit:
CodeRabbit is an AI code review tool that comments on pull requests in GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps and Bitbucket, summarizing changes and pointing out bugs, security issues and style problems.

This list gathers its official documentation, getting-started guides, configuration examples, integrations and tutorials. Use **Configuration Examples** to tune reviews for your codebase; AI reviews work best as a first pass, with a human still approving the merge.
browserify:
Browserify was the first popular tool that let developers use Node.js-style `require()` modules in the browser by bundling them into a single file. It helped make npm the main package registry for front-end code.

Most new projects now use Vite, esbuild, Rollup or webpack, but Browserify is still found in older codebases. This list is useful for maintaining those projects or planning a migration: official docs, transforms, tutorials and tools.
tensorflow-js:
TensorFlow.js runs and trains machine learning models directly in JavaScript, in the browser using WebGL or WebGPU, or in Node.js. It lets you add features like image classification, pose detection or text analysis without sending user data to a server.

This list gathers tutorials, pre-trained models, tools and community projects. Start with **Learn** to load a ready-made model, then move to **Tools** when you need to convert a Python model or train your own.
gamemaker:
GameMaker is a 2D game engine with its own scripting language, GML, used to make hits such as Undertale, Hyper Light Drifter and Hotline Miami. It exports to Windows, macOS, Linux, mobile and consoles.

This is one of the largest lists in the Library: libraries for data structures, timing, async loading, native extensions, debugging and tools. Beginners should begin with **Getting Started**; experienced developers will find reusable code in the later sections.
tailwind-css:
Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework: instead of writing custom classes, you compose designs with small single-purpose classes directly in your HTML or components. It has become one of the most used styling tools in React, Vue, Svelte and Laravel projects.

This list collects useful links, editor extensions, tools, plugins and component libraries. If you want to move faster, browse **UI libraries, components & templates** before building every interface element yourself.
haxe-game-development:
Haxe is a strongly typed language that compiles to many targets, including C++, JavaScript and HashLink. That makes it popular for indie games that need to ship on desktop, web and consoles from one codebase; Dead Cells and Papers, Please were built with Haxe.

This list covers game engines such as HaxeFlixel, Heaps and OpenFL, low-level libraries, physics, networking, storage and example games. Pick an engine first, then use the other sections to fill specific needs.
whisper:
Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model. It transcribes and translates audio in dozens of languages, including Spanish, and runs locally on a laptop or server without sending recordings to the cloud.

This list gathers the official release, faster and smaller variants such as whisper.cpp and faster-whisper, desktop and web apps, CLI tools and packages for developers. If you just want subtitles or meeting notes, start with **Apps**; to integrate it into your own software, go to **Packages**.
steam-2:
Steam is Valve's game distribution platform and also an ecosystem with public APIs, Steamworks for developers, workshop content and a large modding and tools community.

This list focuses on packages and resources for developers: libraries to query the Steam Web API, integrate Steamworks features, read game data and build bots or companion tools. Check each package's maintenance status, since Steam's APIs change over time.
jquery:
jQuery simplified DOM manipulation, events and AJAX for more than a decade, and it still runs on a large share of websites, especially WordPress themes and older business applications.

This list collects plugins for UI, animation, forms, mobile and testing, plus server integrations and community resources. For new projects, modern browsers cover most of what jQuery offered natively, but this collection remains valuable when you maintain or extend an existing site.
neovim:
Neovim is a modern fork of Vim with built-in LSP, Lua configuration, Tree-sitter syntax and an asynchronous plugin system. It has become one of the favourite editors for developers who want a fast, keyboard-driven environment they can shape themselves.

With more than 1,500 entries, this is the largest list in the Library. Organise your setup in order: a **Plugin Manager**, then **LSP** and **Completion**, then language support and the rest. Pre-built distributions are a good shortcut if you don't want to configure everything from zero.
gdpr:
The EU General Data Protection Regulation applies to any product that processes personal data of people in the European Union, wherever the company is based. For developers it means privacy by design, records of processing, security measures, breach notification and respect for user rights.

This list is organized by the articles of the regulation, which makes it a practical checklist. It is useful for product teams and freelancers working with European clients. It is not legal advice; confirm important decisions with a specialist.
evm-security:
The Ethereum Virtual Machine runs smart contracts on Ethereum and many compatible chains. Bugs in those contracts can be exploited instantly and usually cannot be reversed, so security is part of design, not a final step.

This list explains the EVM security landscape: guides, governance, architecture, standards, threats, known vulnerabilities and controls. Read it before deploying contracts that hold value, and combine it with audits and automated analysis tools.
vapor:
Vapor is the most popular web framework for server-side Swift. It lets iOS and macOS developers build APIs, websites and real-time services in the same language they already use, with async/await, an ORM called Fluent and Leaf templates.

This list collects libraries, tools, hosting services, courses and open-source projects built with Vapor. Start with **Education** if you are new to the backend, then look at **Open-source Projects** to see how real apps are structured.
play1-framework:
Play 1 is the original version of the Play Framework, a Java web framework known for hot reloading, a stateless architecture and a convention-over-configuration approach inspired by Rails. Later versions moved to Scala and a different API, so Play 1 applications remain a separate ecosystem.

This list collects modules, plugins and resources for teams still maintaining Play 1 apps. If you are starting a new project, consider a current framework; if you are maintaining one, these modules can save you from rewriting common features.
circuitpython:
CircuitPython is Adafruit's version of Python for microcontrollers. You plug a board into USB, it appears as a drive, and you edit a `code.py` file — no compiler or IDE required. That makes it one of the easiest ways to start with electronics.

This list collects official learning guides, community libraries, frameworks, compatible hardware, videos and books. Beginners should start with the **Adafruit Learning System Guides**, which pair each project with the exact parts you need.
d3:
D3.js is the JavaScript library behind many of the most original data visualizations on the web. Instead of fixed chart types, it binds data to SVG, Canvas or HTML elements so you can design exactly the graphic you need.

This list gathers chart libraries built on D3, mapping tools, utilities, server-side rendering and example galleries. If you only need standard charts, a higher-level library from **Charts** will be faster; use D3 directly when you need full control.
libgdx:
libGDX is a Java game framework that targets Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS and the web from one codebase. It gives you low-level control over rendering, input, audio and physics, and has been used for many commercial indie games.

This list collects official resources, tutorials, free assets, community channels and related lists. Kotlin developers can use it too through KTX extensions. Start with **Tutorials** if this is your first game with the framework.
theoretical-computer-science:
Theoretical computer science studies what can be computed and how efficiently: algorithms, complexity classes, computability, logic, cryptography and quantum computing. It is the mathematical foundation behind everyday software engineering.

This list gathers free lecture notes, recorded university courses, books and handbooks. Students preparing for exams or graduate studies should start with the **Introductory** material and the video playlists, then move into specific areas such as complexity and computability.
sass:
Sass is a CSS preprocessor that adds variables, nesting, mixins, functions and modules to CSS. It is still widely used in design systems and frameworks such as Bootstrap, even as native CSS adds features like custom properties and nesting.

This list explains the difference between Sass and SCSS syntax and collects frameworks, mixin libraries, style guides, articles, tools and books. If you are starting a new project, check which features you really need before adding a build step.
qlik:
Qlik is a business intelligence platform for dashboards, data exploration and reporting, with products such as Qlik Sense and QlikView and an associative engine that makes it easy to explore relationships between data.

This list collects official documentation, community blogs, books and extensions. It is useful for analysts building dashboards and for developers integrating Qlik into other applications through its APIs and mashups.
ffmpeg:
FFmpeg is the command-line toolkit behind much of the world's video and audio processing. It records, converts, cuts, compresses and streams almost any media format, and powers tools like VLC, OBS and many streaming services.

This list gathers documentation, JavaScript and native bindings, mobile builds, tutorials and community resources. If the command syntax feels difficult, begin with **Tutorials**, which explain the most common recipes step by step.
frameworks:
This list compares CSS frameworks by approach: resets and normalizers, class-less frameworks that style plain HTML, very lightweight options, general-purpose frameworks, Material Design implementations and utility-based systems.

It is useful when choosing a styling base for a new site. Class-less and lightweight frameworks suit documentation and small projects; general-purpose and utility frameworks scale better for applications. The last section lists projects that are no longer maintained, so you can avoid them.
